title: Chess AI
description: Play chess against a computer that picks random moves, challenge a friend, or watch two bots battle on a wooden board, free in your browser.
about:
Chess AI is a relaxed, good-looking chess board with a wooden frame and smooth sliding pieces. Tap a piece and every legal square lights up, while tiny icons on each tile show which pieces can reach it, so it is easy to see threats and plan captures at a glance.

The rules are real chess: moves that would leave your king in check are blocked, and castling, en passant and pawn promotion to a queen all work. By default you play White against a computer opponent that chooses random legal moves, which makes it a friendly sparring partner rather than a grandmaster.

The Auto switches let the computer play either side, so you can hand both colours to a friend on the same device or sit back and watch a bot-versus-bot game at up to 20 moves per second. It is ideal for beginners learning how pieces move and for anyone who wants a quick, casual game.
howToPlay: You play White and move first: tap one of your pieces to see its legal moves, then tap a highlighted square to move or capture. Black answers automatically when its Auto switch is on. Checkmate the enemy king to win; if a side has no legal moves and is not in check, the game is a stalemate.

controls.action: Select a piece and show its moves
Let the computer play White or Black
Set the computer's moves per second
Flip the board to White or Black

tips: Watch the small piece icons on each square: they show which pieces from both sides can move to or capture there.
The computer moves at random, so set simple traps and it will often walk right into them.
Turn off Black's Auto switch to play a friend on the same screen, taking turns with the pieces.
Switch both Auto kings on and pick 20 APS to watch a full random game play out in seconds.

faq.question: Is Chess AI free to play?
faq.answer: Yes. It is completely free and runs in your browser with no download or sign-up.

faq.question: Can I play on a phone or tablet?
faq.answer: Yes. Tap a piece and then a highlighted square to move; the board scales to fit phone and tablet screens.

faq.question: How strong is the computer opponent?
faq.answer: Not strong at all: it picks a random legal move each turn, so it is best for learning and casual games rather than serious training.
